The Story of Vrushabsen the Merchant's Son

I bow to Lord Jina, who bestows the happiness of heaven and liberation and is worshipped by the entire world, and I write the story of Vrushabsen.

In Pataliputra (Patna), there lived a merchant named Vrushabdatt. Through the merit of past lives, he had great wealth. His wife was Vrushabdatta, and they had a son named Vrushabsen, who was endowed with all good qualities. Vrushabsen was very righteous and always practised meritorious deeds like charity and worship.

Vrushabsen's maternal uncle Dhanpati had a wife named Shrikanta, and they had a daughter named Dhanashri. Dhanashri was beautiful, clever, and educated. She was married to Vrushabsen. The couple lived happily, with all manner of sensual pleasures always at their disposal.

One day, Vrushabsen went to see the monk Damdhar Muni. With devotion, he worshipped him and heard his sacred discourse on dharma. The discourse pleased him greatly and had a profound effect on him. At that very moment, he became detached from the world and the sensual pleasures that appeared as happiness through delusion. He went to the monk and took Jain initiation for the sake of his soul's welfare.

His young wife Dhanashri was greatly distressed at his taking initiation in his youth. She could think of nothing but weeping day and night. Her father Dhanpati could not bear her grief. He went to the meditation grove, brought Vrushabsen back by force, and broke his monastic vows, making him a householder again. Truly, deluded people, without considering what should and should not be done, act like madmen, binding intense sinful karma.

Just as a person is forced to remain in prison, so Vrushabsen had to stay at home for some time. After that, he became a monk again. When Dhanpati learned of this, he brought Vrushabsen home by some pretext and this time bound him with iron chains. The monk thought, "This man will again push me down from the mountain of vows, will break my vow." So he took the vow of sallekhana (fast unto death) and in that very state left his body. Through the ripening of merit, he was reborn as a god in heaven.

However much the wicked may torment the good, the pure-minded never engage in sinful actions. The wicked man may cause great trouble, but the pure soul remains steadfast in dharma.

This story teaches that worldly attachments, even from loved ones, can be the greatest obstacle to spiritual progress. Vrushabsen's father-in-law, though motivated by love for his daughter, committed a grave sin by forcibly breaking a monk's vows. The wise should understand that true love supports the spiritual journey, not obstructs it. And those who are called to the monastic life should protect their vows with determination, even in the face of family pressure.
